sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821

items.q: Acidemia is defined as blood pH:
items.exp: Acidemia: blood pH < 7.36; alkalemia: blood pH > 7.44. (Book p821)

items.q: Alkalemia is defined as blood pH:
Match the terminology box — 1) Acidemia  2) Acidosis  3) Alkalemia  4) Alkalosis … A) If alkalemia left unopposed  B) Blood pH < 7.36  C) If acidemia left unopposed  D) Blood pH > 7.44
items.exp: Acidemia = pH < 7.36; acidosis = if acidemia left unopposed. Alkalemia = pH > 7.44; alkalosis = if alkalemia left unopposed. (Book p821)

items.q: ‘Acidemia and acidosis mean exactly the same thing, and so do alkalemia and alkalosis.’
opts: False — acidemia/alkalemia are the pH findings; acidosis/alkalosis are those states left unopposed
True — the terms are used interchangeably in the chapter
False — acidosis refers only to a raised PaCO₂
True, but only for respiratory disorders
items.exp: The distinction is printed: acidemia = pH < 7.36 and acidosis = if acidemia is left unopposed; likewise for alkalemia/alkalosis. (Book p821)

items.q: At pH 7.4 the H⁺ concentration is 40 nmol/L. Using the printed multipliers, H⁺ at pH 7.3 is:
items.exp: Moving 0.1 pH below 7.4 multiplies H⁺ by 1.25: 40 × 1.25 = 50 nmol/L. (Book p821)

items.q: Using the same multipliers, H⁺ at pH 7.2 is:
items.exp: Two 0.1-pH steps below 7.4: 40 × 1.25 × 1.25 = 63 nmol/L (the printed value at pH 7.2). (Book p821)

items.q: Moving 0.1 pH above 7.4, the printed multiplier is ×0.8 — so H⁺ at pH 7.5 is:
items.exp: × 0.8 per 0.1 pH rise: 40 × 0.8 = 32 nmol/L at pH 7.5. (Book p821)

items.q: H⁺ concentration printed at pH 7.6 is:
items.exp: The printed ladder is pH 7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.4 = 40, 7.5 = 32 and 7.6 = 25 nmol/L. (Book p821)

items.q: Match the pH and H⁺ pairs printed in the H⁺ ion estimation diagram — 1) pH 7.2  2) pH 7.3  3) pH 7.5  4) pH 7.6 … A) 25 nmol/L  B) 63 nmol/L  C) 32 nmol/L  D) 50 nmol/L
items.exp: Printed pairs: pH 7.2 → 63, pH 7.3 → 50, pH 7.4 → 40, pH 7.5 → 32, pH 7.6 → 25 nmol/L. (Book p821)

items.q: A resident estimates H⁺ as 40 nmol/L and notes the patient's pH is 7.3. Would you correct the resident?
opts: Yes — at pH 7.3 H⁺ should be 50 nmol/L (×1.25 per 0.1 pH fall)
No — 40 nmol/L holds for any pH between 7.2 and 7.6
Yes — at pH 7.3 H⁺ should be 63 nmol/L
No — the estimate is valid because pH and H⁺ are unrelated
items.exp: 40 nmol/L is the value at pH 7.4; each 0.1 pH fall multiplies H⁺ by 1.25, giving 50 nmol/L at pH 7.3. (Book p821)
